title: At-Least-Once with Redis Streams
description: How I built retries and persistence into a Go task queue.
intro: Building PierceMQ taught me how much work hides behind "just deliver the task". This post walks through the delivery semantics I chose and why.
lead: The core promise is simple: every enqueued job runs at least once, even if workers crash mid-flight. Everything else — retries, persistence, redelivery — follows from that promise.
body:
## Consumer groups

Consumer groups give us pending entries, acknowledgements, and redelivery for free. Each worker owns a subset of the stream, and unacknowledged messages show up in the pending list.

```go
// Claim a batch and process each message.
msgs, err := rdb.XReadGroup(ctx, &redis.XReadGroupArgs{
    Group:    "workers",
    Consumer: hostname,
    Streams:  []string{"jobs", ">"},
}).Result()
```

## Retries

Failed jobs go back on the stream with a backoff counter in the payload. After N attempts the job moves to a dead-letter stream for inspection instead of poisoning the queue.
outro: Delivery semantics are a design choice, not a default. Pick at-least-once when duplicates are cheap and loss is not. Thanks for reading — happy queueing!

title: Thinking in Messages with Bubble Tea
description: Elm-style TUI design from building a Docker monitor.
intro: Contyard is a real-time Docker TUI built with Bubble Tea. The biggest shift from normal Go programs was modelling everything — ticks, keypresses, Docker events — as messages.
lead: In the Elm architecture there is exactly one loop: receive a message, update the model, render a view. Once that clicks, TUI code stops being spaghetti and starts being a state machine.
outro: Messages all the way down — it scales further than you'd expect. Thanks for reading, and have fun in the terminal!

title: Postgres Indexes I Actually Use
description: B-tree, GIN, and partial indexes with real query plans.
intro: Most queries I write only need three index shapes. This is the short list I reach for before touching anything exotic.
lead: An index is a bet about which rows a query will touch. The cheapest way to win that bet is to look at the query plan first and index what the filter actually needs.
body:
## B-tree

The default. Great for equality and ranges. If your `WHERE` clause filters on a column, a B-tree on that column is the first thing to try.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_status ON jobs (status);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending';
```

## GIN

Full-text search and JSONB containment. A GIN index turns `@@` and `@>` queries from sequential scans into index lookups.

## Partial

Index only the hot rows and watch the size drop. `WHERE status = 'pending'` on the index keeps it small when most rows are already done.
outro: Index the filter, verify with EXPLAIN, and stop there until measurements say otherwise. Thanks for reading!

title: Designing CLI Flags People Remember
description: Lessons from reimplementing wc in Go.
intro: WCTool is a tiny Go reimplementation of `wc`. Its smallness made every flag decision visible — a good microscope for CLI design.
lead: The first rule I kept relearning: match expectations before being clever. `wc` with no flags prints lines, words, and bytes, so mine does too.
outro: Small tools, sharp flags. Thanks for reading — may your CLIs compose cleanly!

title: Histograms in the Terminal
description: Text-based charts for quick dataset sanity checks.
intro: PrepPulse renders histograms with block characters for quick data sanity checks — no notebook required. Here's how the rendering works.
lead: A terminal histogram has two jobs: show the shape of the distribution and fit in 80 columns. Bin counts derived from the data range do both better than any magic number.
body:
## Binning

Pick bin counts from the data range, not from a magic number. A constant bin width keeps bars comparable across runs.

```go
width := (max - min) / float64(bins)
idx := int((v - min) / width)
counts[min(idx, bins-1)]++
```

## Rendering

Scale bars to the terminal width so output stays readable. Block characters give roughly eight levels of vertical resolution per row.
outro: Next time a CSV looks suspicious, histogram it before you open anything heavier. Thanks for reading!

title: A* Search, Visualized
description: Watching open and closed sets expand toward the goal.
intro: An early algorithms project: pick start and end points, watch A* expand toward the shortest path. The visualization taught me more than the textbook did.
lead: The heuristic is the whole algorithm. With a good estimate the search marches straight at the goal; with a bad one it degrades into flooding the grid.
body:
## Open set

A priority queue ordered by f = g + h, where g is the cost so far and h is the heuristic estimate to the goal.

```python
open_set = [(heuristic(start), start)]
heapq.heapify(open_set)
```

## Closed set

Never re-expand a node with a better known path. The closed set is what keeps the search from wandering in circles.
outro: Play with the heuristic and watch the search change character entirely. Thanks for reading!

title: Backtracking Through Sudoku
description: Recursion and constraint propagation, step by step.
intro: A Sudoku solver with a Pygame GUI — an early project for practicing recursion. The algorithm is three lines; the insight is one word: undo.
lead: Try a digit, recurse, undo. The undo is the algorithm. Everything else is pruning the search so the undo happens less often.
body:
## Pruning

Check row, column, and box before recursing deeper. Each failed check avoids an entire subtree of wasted guesses.

```python
def solve(board):
    cell = find_empty(board)
    if cell is None:
        return True
    for digit in candidates(board, cell):
        board[cell] = digit
        if solve(board):
            return True
        board[cell] = 0  # undo
    return False
```

## Ordering

Fill the most constrained cell first. Fewer candidates means less branching, which compounds at every level.
outro: Recursion plus undo solves a surprising number of puzzles. Thanks for reading!

title: From Flask to Go APIs
description: What changed when I rewrote a small API in Go.
intro: The WeatherApp rewrite from Flask to Go forced explicit error handling everywhere. Here's what survived the translation and what didn't.
lead: Flask hides the request lifecycle behind decorators and globals; Go hands you `(w, r)` and wishes you luck. The explicitness is verbose at first and clarifying forever.
outro: Explicit over magical — at least for APIs I have to maintain. Thanks for reading!

title: Docker Layer Caching for Go Builds
description: Multi-stage builds that keep deploys fast.
intro: Slow Docker builds are usually a layer-ordering problem. For Go services the fix is small and mechanical.
lead: Order your Dockerfile by change frequency: dependencies first, source last. Layers that rarely change stay cached, and rebuilds only redo the final steps.
body:
## Modules first

Copy `go.mod` and download deps before the source. Editing code no longer invalidates the dependency layer.

```dockerfile
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . ./
RUN go build -o /app/web ./cmd/web
```

## Multi-stage

Build in one stage, ship a minimal binary in the next. The runtime image holds the binary and nothing else.
outro: Cache the stable layers, rebuild only the code. Thanks for reading — may your deploys stay fast!

title: HTMX Instead of an SPA
description: Why server-rendered partials won for this site.
intro: This site is server-rendered Go with HTMX for partial swaps. No build step, no client router — and deliberately so.
lead: The server owns the state and the browser swaps HTML. For content-heavy pages with islands of interactivity, that division of labour wins on simplicity.
body:
## Less state There is no client store to keep in sync because there is no client model. Each swap replaces a fragment and inherits server truth. ```html
Contyard
``` ## When not to Reach for an SPA when offline support or deep client state is required. The rest of the time, HTML over the wire is enough.
outro: Use the smallest tool that fits the job. Thanks for reading, and enjoy the fast pages!
